'''Daniel Hunt Janzen''' (born January 18, 1939)<ref name="Interview"/> is an American [[Evolutionary ecology|evolutionary ecologist]] and [[Conservation movement|conservationist]]. He divides his time between his professorship in [[biology]] at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he is the DiMaura Professor of Conservation Biology, and his research and field work in [[Costa Rica]].

Janzen and his wife [[Winifred Hallwachs]] have catalogued the biodiversity of Costa Rica. Through a [[DNA barcoding]] initiative, Janzen and geneticist [[Paul D. N. Hebert|Paul Hebert]] have registered over 500,000 specimens representing more than 45,000 species, which has led to the identification of [[cryptic species]] of near-identical appearance that differ in terms of genetics and ecological niche. Janzen and Hallwachs developed some of the most influential hypotheses in ecology that continue to influence research more than 50 years later.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />
 
Janzen and Hallwachs helped to establish the [[Area de Conservación Guanacaste World Heritage Site]], one of the oldest, largest and most successful [[habitat restoration]] projects in the world.

== Early life and education==
Daniel Hunt Janzen was born January 18, 1939, in [[Milwaukee]], [[Wisconsin]].<ref name="Interview">{{cite web |title=Prof. Daniel H. Janzen Interview Summary |url=http://www.af-info.jp/better_future/html/vol_V/2014/Prof_Janzen/2014b_Janzen1.html |website=Blue Planet Prize: A better future for the planet Earth |access-date=November 2, 2019}}</ref> His father, Daniel Hugo Janzen,<ref>{{cite news |title=Mrs. Floyd Janzen |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/19361970/the_greenville_news/ |access-date=November 2, 2019 |work=The Greenville News|location=Greenville, South Carolina |date=May 8, 1980|page=78}}</ref> grew up in a [[Mennonite]] farming community and served as Director of the [[United States Fish and Wildlife Service]].<ref name="Interview"/> His father and mother, Miss Floyd Clark Foster of [[Greenville, South Carolina]], were married on April 29, 1937.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Changes Name|journal=The Survey |date=May 1937 |location=Washington, D.C.|volume=13|number=3–4 |page=99 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1P3lG_3LtOUC&pg=RA5-PA99}}</ref>

Janzen obtained his [[Bachelor of Science|B.Sc.]] degree in biology from the [[University of Minnesota]] in 1961, and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1965.<ref name="Becher"/>

==Career ==
In 1963, Janzen attended a two-month course in tropical biology taught in several field sites throughout [[Costa Rica]]. This Advanced Science Seminar in Tropical Biology was the precursor to a Fundamentals in Tropical Biology course, which Janzen designed for the [[Organization for Tropical Studies]] (OTS), a consortium of several North American and Costa Rican universities. Janzen went back in 1965 as an instructor and has lectured in at least one of the three yearly courses every year since.<ref name="Becher">{{cite book |last1=Becher |first1=Anne |last2=McClure |first2=Kyle |last3=White Scheuering |first3=Rachel |last4=Willis |first4=Julia |chapter=Janzen, Daniel H. |title=American environmental leaders: from colonial times to the present |date=2000 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |location=Santa Barbara, Calif. |pages=426–427|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s2pYAAAAYAAJ&q=Daniel+Hunt+Janzen+18+jan+1939|isbn=978-1-59237-119-8 }}</ref>

Janzen taught at the [[University of Kansas]] (1965–1968), the [[University of Chicago]] (1969–1972), and the [[University of Michigan]] (1972–1976) before joining the faculty at the [[University of Pennsylvania]].<ref name="BBVA">{{cite web |title=Daniel H. Janzen – Frontiers of Knowledge Laureate |url=https://www.fbbva.es/en/galardonados/daniel-h-janzen-2/https://www.fbbva.es/en/galardonados/daniel-h-janzen-2/ |website=Fundación BBVA |access-date=October 24, 2019 }}{{Dead link|date=January 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>  There he is the DiMaura Professor of Conservation Biology, and his research and field work in [[Costa Rica]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Presentation by Tropical Biologist Dr Janzen |url=http://www.pennclubchicago.com/s/1587/gid2/16/interior_1col.aspx?sid=1587&gid=6&pgid=15218&crid=0&calpgid=2515&calcid=9700 |website=Penn Club of Chicago |access-date=October 17, 2019}}</ref>

Janzen has also held teaching positions in [[Venezuela]] ([[Universidad de Oriente]], [[Cumaná]] in 1965–66; [[University of the Andes (Venezuela)|Universidad de los Los Andes, Mérida]] in 1973), and in [[Puerto Rico]] ([[Universidad de Puerto Rico]], [[Río Piedras]], 1969).<ref name="Ciencias">{{cite web |title=Daniel H. Janzen Académico Correspondiente |url=http://www.anc.cr/index.php/miembros/team/daniel-h-janzen |website=Academia Nacional de Ciencias |access-date=October 24, 2019 |archive-date=October 24, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191024144022/http://www.anc.cr/index.php/miembros/team/daniel-h-janzen }}</ref>

== Área del Conservación de Guanacaste (ACG) ==
The [[Guanacaste Conservation Area|Área de Conservación de Guanacaste (ACG)]] is a prominent conservation area in northwestern Costa Rica, encompassing over 163,000 hectares of diverse ecosystems, including tropical dry forests, rainforests, and marine areas. Established in the 1990s, the ACG unifies several national parks, such as Santa Rosa, Guanacaste, Rincón de la Vieja, and Junquillal Bay, into a single administrative entity. This integration aims to protect and restore the region's unique biodiversity and facilitate natural ecosystem regeneration. The ACG is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, highlighting its global ecological significance and Costa Rica's commitment to environmental conservation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Guanacaste Conservation Area and Its UNESCO World Heritage Status – Green Circle Experience |url=https://greencircleexperience.com/2024/12/31/the-guanacaste-conservation-area-and-its-unesco-world-heritage-status/ |access-date=2024-12-31 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Dr. Daniel Janzen, recognizing the necessity for a cohesive conservation strategy in Guanacaste, along with his wife, biologist Dr. Winnie Hallwachs, championed the establishment of a contiguous conservation area to facilitate natural ecosystem regeneration.

Their comprehensive strategy encompassed several key initiatives:

* '''Restoring Tropical Dry Forests:''' Acquiring degraded pastures and enabling the recovery of natural vegetation.
* '''Integrating Local Communities:''' Training local residents to serve as park guards, educators, and conservation advocates.
* '''Fundraising for Land Purchases:''' Securing donations and forming partnerships with international organizations to purchase private lands and integrate them into the protected area.

==Research==
Janzen's early work focused on the careful and meticulous documentation of species in Costa Rica, and in particular on ecological processes and the dynamics and evolution of animal-plant interactions.<ref name="Becher"/>{{rp|426}} <ref name="Mitchell"/>
In 1967, for example he described the phenological specialization of bee-pollinated species of Bignoniaceae,<ref>Janzen, D. H. 1967. Synchronization of sexual reproduction of trees within the dry season in Central America. Evolution 21: 620-637.</ref> amongst them a "kind of mass flowering", which Alwyn Howard Gentry in his classification of flowering named Type 4 or "big bang" strategy.<ref>Alwyn H. Gentry. Flowering Phenology and Diversity in Tropical Bignoniaceae. Biotropica 6(1): 64-68 1974</ref> Janzen proposed many hypotheses that inspired decades of work by tropical and temperate ecologists (see below).

[[Miguel Altieri]] in his textbook ''Agroecology: The Science of Sustainable Agriculture'' says: "Janzen's 1973 article on tropical agroecosystems was the first widely read evaluation of why tropical agricultural systems might function differently from those of the temperate zones".<ref name="Altieri">{{cite book |last1=Altieri |first1=Miguel |title=Agroecology: the science of sustainable agriculture |date=October 13, 1995 |publisher=Westview Press |isbn=0-8133-1718-5 |page=23 |edition=2nd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-tJMDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT23}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janzen |first1=D. H. |title=Tropical Agroecosystems: These habitats are misunderstood by the temperate zones, mismanaged by the tropics |journal=Science |date=December 21, 1973 |volume=182 |issue=4118 |pages=1212–1219 |doi=10.1126/science.182.4118.1212 |pmid=17811308 |s2cid=12290280 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/284405310 |access-date=November 2, 2019}}</ref>

In 1985, realizing that the area in which they worked was threatened, Janzen and Hallwachs expanded the focus of their work to include tropical forest restoration, expansion (through land purchases) and conservation.<ref name="Pringle">{{cite journal |last1=Pringle |first1=Robert M. |title=Upgrading protected areas to conserve wild biodiversity |journal=Nature |date=June 1, 2017 |volume=546 |issue=7656 |pages=91–99 |doi=10.1038/nature22902 |pmid=28569807 |bibcode=2017Natur.546...91P |s2cid=4387383 }}</ref><ref name="Singer"/> They employed the help of local Costa Ricans, converting their farming skills into [[parataxonomy]], a term they coined in the late 1980s.<ref name="Allen" /><ref name=":0">Kazmier, Robin (June 15, 2017). "[https://cmsw.mit.edu/parataxonomist-revolution-group-rural-costa-ricans-discovered-10000-new-species/ The Parataxonomist Revolution: How a Group of Rural Costa Ricans Discovered 10,000 New Species]". ''Comparative Media Studies: Science Writing''.</ref> As of 2017, some 10,000 new species in the [[Area de Conservación Guanacaste World Heritage Site|Area de Conservacion Guanacaste]] have been identified thanks to the efforts of parataxonomists.<ref name=":0" />

Through a [[DNA barcoding]] initiative with [[geneticist]] [[Paul D. N. Hebert|Paul Hebert]], they have registered over 500,000 specimens representing more than 45,000 species, which has led to the identification of [[cryptic species]] of near-identical appearance that differ in terms of genetics and ecological niche.<ref name="Davis">{{cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Tinsley H. |title=Profile of Daniel H. Janzen |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=September 26, 2017 |volume=114 |issue=39 |pages=10300–10302 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1714623114 |pmid=28893992 |pmc=5625942 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Halloway">{{cite web |last1=Halloway |first1=M. |title=Democratizing Taxonomy|date=July 29, 2008 |url=https://www.conservationmagazine.org/2008/07/democratizing-taxonomy/ |website=Conservation magazine |access-date=October 18, 2019}}</ref><ref name="Hebert">{{cite journal |last1=Hebert |first1=P. D. N. |last2=Penton |first2=E. H. |last3=Burns |first3=J. M. |last4=Janzen |first4=D. H. |last5=Hallwachs |first5=W. |title=Ten species in one: DNA barcoding reveals cryptic species in the neotropical skipper butterfly Astraptes fulgerator |journal=PNAS |date=2004 |volume=101 |issue=41 |pages=14812–14817 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0406166101 |pmid=15465915 |pmc=522015 |bibcode=2004PNAS..10114812H |doi-access=free }}</ref> Janzen and Hallwachs have supported species barcoding initiatives at both national and international levels through the [[Instituto Nacional de Biodiversidad]] (INBio), CBOL ([[Consortium for the Barcode of Life]]) and iBOL ([[International Barcode of Life]]).<ref>{{cite web |title=Koerner Lecture to examine conservation of wild biodiversity via biodiversity development |url=http://yfile.news.yorku.ca/2017/03/20/koerner-lecture-to-examine-conservation-of-wild-biodiversity-via-biodiversity-development/ |website=York University |date=March 20, 2017 |access-date=October 17, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janzen |first1=D.H. |last2=Hallwachs |first2=W. |title=How a country can DNA barcode itself |journal=Barcode Bulletin|publisher = IBOL |date=October 2, 2019 |doi=10.21083/ibol.v9i1.5526 |url=https://ibol.org/barcodebulletin/features/how-a-tropical-country-can-dna-barcode-itself/|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Wolf2008">{{cite magazine |last1=Wolf |first1=G. |title=A Simple Plan to ID Every Creature on Earth |url=https://www.wired.com/2008/09/ff-barcode/ |access-date=October 15, 2019 |magazine=Wired |date=September 22, 2008}}</ref>

=== Influential hypotheses ===
Janzen is known for proposing "characteristically imaginative and unorthodox" hypotheses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sherratt |first1=Thomas N. |last2=Wilkinson |first2=David M. |last3=Bain |first3=Roderick S. |date=February 25, 2006 |title=Why fruits rot, seeds mold and meat spoils: A reappraisal |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304380005003753 |journal=Ecological Modelling |volume=192 |issue=3 |pages=618–626 |doi=10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2005.07.030 |issn=0304-3800|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These hypotheses have received varying degrees of support,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Currie |first=David J. |date=2017 |title=Mountain passes are higher not only in the tropics |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ecog.02695 |journal=Ecography |language=en |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=459–460 |doi=10.1111/ecog.02695 |issn=0906-7590|url-access=subscription }}</ref> but are notable for having inspired a large and sustained body of research, as evidenced by the extremely high citation rates of many of his papers for decades after they are published.<ref name=":2" />

One of Janzen's most famous ideas (from his most highly cited paper)<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Daniel H. Janzen |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=zwSlbVwAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao |access-date=November 29, 2023 |website=scholar.google.com |archive-date=December 28, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241228070810/https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=zwSlbVwAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao }}</ref> is now known as the [[Janzen–Connell hypothesis|Janzen-Connell hypothesis]], as Janzen and [[Joseph H. Connell|Joseph Connell]] independently proposed the idea in 1970-1971. They both suggested that the high diversity of tropical trees was due, in part, to specialist enemies attacking seeds or seedlings that were particularly close to the parent tree or particularly densely clustered, thus preventing any one species from becoming dominant.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Janzen |first=Daniel H. |date=1970 |title=Herbivores and the Number of Tree Species in Tropical Forests |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/282687 |journal=The American Naturalist |language=en |volume=104 |issue=940 |pages=501–528 |doi=10.1086/282687 |issn=0003-0147|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Another influential idea<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Sheldon |first1=Kimberly S. |last2=Huey |first2=Raymond B. |last3=Kaspari |first3=Michael |last4=Sanders |first4=Nathan J. |date=2018 |title=Fifty Years of Mountain Passes: A Perspective on Dan Janzen's Classic Article |url=http://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/697046 |journal=The American Naturalist |language=en |volume=191 |issue=5 |pages=553–565 |doi=10.1086/697046 |pmid=29693443 |issn=0003-0147|url-access=subscription }}</ref> comes from Janzen's 1967 paper 'Why mountain passes are higher in the tropics'.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Janzen |first=Daniel H. |date=1967 |title=Why Mountain Passes are Higher in the Tropics |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/282487 |journal=The American Naturalist |language=en |volume=101 |issue=919 |pages=233–249 |doi=10.1086/282487 |issn=0003-0147|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It proposes that tropical mountains are more of a barrier to species dispersal than temperate mountains because tropical species are less able to tolerate changes in temperature with elevation, having evolved and lived in relatively stable climates.

In a 1977 paper 'Why fruits rot, seeds mould, and meat spoils',<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Janzen |first=Daniel H. |date=1977 |title=Why Fruits Rot, Seeds Mold, and Meat Spoils |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=111 |issue=980 |pages=691–713 |doi=10.1086/283200 |jstor=2460325 |issn=0003-0147}}</ref> Janzen proposed that microbes render food inedible (or at least distasteful) to vertebrates not just as a by product of microbe-microbe competition or accidental waste products, but as an evolutionary strategy to repel vertebrates consumers, who would otherwise eat the food resource and the microbes themselves. Evidence is mixed, and it is hard to test whether compounds evolved to deter other microbes or vertebrates,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kupferschmidt |first=Kai |date=March 11, 2014 |title=Rotten Fruit May Be Due to Microbe Warfare |work=Science |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/rotten-fruit-may-be-due-microbe-warfare}}</ref> but the idea has been widely incorporated into studies of vertebrate feeding from humans<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Speth |first1=John D. |last2=Eugène |first2=Morin |date=October 27, 2022 |title=Putrid Meat in the Tropics: It Wasn't Just For Inuit |url=https://paleoanthropology.org/ojs/index.php/paleo/article/view/114 |journal=PaleoAnthropology |language=en |volume=2022 |issue=2 |doi=10.48738/2022.iss2.114 |issn=1545-0031}}</ref> to dinosaurs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kane |first1=Adam |last2=Healy |first2=Kevin |last3=Ruxton |first3=Graeme D. |date=February 1, 2023 |title=Was Allosaurus really predominantly a scavenger? |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304380022003453 |journal=Ecological Modelling |volume=476 |article-number=110247 |doi=10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2022.110247 |issn=0304-3800|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Coevolution of plants and animals===
* [[Coevolution]] of a mutualistic system in New World tropics between species of ''[[Acacia]]'' ([[Mimosoideae]]; [[Leguminosae]]), v. gr., ''[[Acacia cornigera]]'', and the ant ''[[Pseudomyrmex ferruginea]]'' ([[Formicidae]]). ''Acacia'' spp in the Neotropics are protected by ants against defoliation; for this, the ants are rewarded by means of special organs and physiology that ''Acacia'' has evolved.<ref name="Becher"/>{{rp|426}}
* ''[[Spondias mombin]]'' ([[Anacardiaceae]]) lost its megafauna seed dispersers in the [[Pleistocene]]. Between fire in open pastures and [[seed predation]] by [[Bean weevil|bruchid beetles]] in closed-canopy forest, ''S. mombin'' does not stand a chance. But, today, in Guanacaste, seeds are dispersed by deer and some 15 other mammals, that feed mostly in forest edges, where bruchids are less likely to find the seeds and fires are not so frequent.<ref name="Mitchell">{{cite journal |last1=Mitchell |first1=John D. |last2=Daly |first2=Douglas C. |title=A revision of Spondias L. (Anacardiaceae) in the Neotropics |journal=PhytoKeys |date=August 5, 2015 |issue=55 |pages=1–92 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.55.8489 |pmid=26312044 |pmc=4547026 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Tropical habitat restoration===
[[Tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forests|Tropical dry forests]] are the world's most threatened forest ecosystems. In middle America there were 550 000&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup> of dry forests at the beginning of the 16th century; today, less than 0.08% (440&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>) remains.<ref name="Wilson">{{cite book |last1=Janzen |first1=Daniel H. |editor-last1=Wilson |editor-first1=EO |editor-last2=Peter |editor-first2=FM |title=Biodiversity |chapter=Chapter 14 Tropical Dry Forests The Most Endangered Major Tropical Ecosystem |date=1988 |publisher=National Academies Press (US) |location=Washington (DC) |chapter-url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK219281/}}</ref> They have been cleared, burnt and replaced by pastures for cattle raising,<ref name="Burgos">{{cite journal |last1=Burgos |first1=Ana |last2=Maass |first2=J.Manuel |title=Vegetation change associated with land-use in tropical dry forest areas of Western Mexico |journal=Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment |date=December 2004 |volume=104 |issue=3 |pages=475–481 |doi=10.1016/j.agee.2004.01.038 }}</ref> at an ever-faster rate during the last 500 years.<ref name="Wilson"/>

In 1985, realizing that widespread development in northwestern Costa Rica was rapidly decimating the forest in which they conducted their research, Janzen and Hallwachs  expanded the focus of their work. Janzen and his wife helped to establish the [[Area de Conservación Guanacaste World Heritage Site]] (ACG), one of the oldest, largest and most successful [[habitat restoration]] projects in the world. They began with the [[Parque Nacional Santa Rosa]], which included {{convert|100|km2|acres|abbr=on}} of pasture and relictual neotropical dry forest and {{convert|230|km2|acres|abbr=on}} of marine habitat.<ref name="Pringle"/> This eventually became the  [[Guanacaste National Park (Costa Rica)|Área de Conservación Guanacaste]], located just south of the Costa Rica-[[Nicaragua]] border, between the Pacific Ocean and the [[Cordillera de Tilaran]] which integrated four different national parks. Together these house at least 15 different [[biotope]]s (namely [[mangroves]], dry forest and shrubs; ephemeral, rainy season, and permanent streams; [[Swamp|fresh water]] and [[Salt marsh|littoral swamps]]; [[tropical rainforest|evergreen rainforests]] and [[cloud forests]], etc.), holding approximately 4% of the world's plant, mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish, and insect diversity, all within an area of less than {{convert|169,000|ha|acres}}.<ref name="Area">{{cite web |title=ACG Biodiversity |url=http://www.gdfcf.org/content/where-we-work |website= Guanacaste Dry Forest Conservation Fund |access-date=October 24, 2019}}</ref> It is one of the oldest, largest and most successful [[habitat restoration]] projects in the world. As of 2019, it consists of {{convert|169,000|ha|acres}}.<ref name="Area"/> The park exemplifies their beliefs about how a park should be run. It is known as a center of biological research, [[forest restoration]] and [[science outreach|community outreach]].<ref name="Davis"/>

Habitat restoration is not a simple matter. Not only must one fight against hundreds of years of ecological degradation, manifested in the form of altered drainage patterns, hard-to-eradicate pastures, [[soil compaction|compacted soils]], exhausted seed banks, diminished adult and [[propagule]] stocks, and the proliferation of fire-resistant and unpalatable weeds from the Old World tropics and subtropics.<ref name="Gomiero">{{cite journal |last1=Gomiero |first1=Tiziano |title=Soil Degradation, Land Scarcity and Food Security: Reviewing a Complex Challenge |journal=Sustainability |date=March 18, 2016 |volume=8 |issue=3 |page=281 |doi=10.3390/su8030281 |doi-access=free }}</ref> 
One is also faced with the difficulties of changing a culture that coevolved with, profited from, and can become miserable with such a system.<ref name="Costanza">{{cite book |last1=Costanza |first1=Robert |last2=Cumberland |first2=John |last3=Daly |first3=Herman |last4=Goodland |first4=Robert |last5=Norgaard |first5=Richard |title=An Introduction to ecological economics |date=1997 |publisher=St. Lucie Press |isbn=1-884015-72-7 |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoec0000unse_q2b0 |url-access=registration }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=van den Bergh |first1=Jeroen C. J. M. |title=Evolutionary thinking in environmental economics |journal=Journal of Evolutionary Economics |date=February 14, 2007 |volume=17 |issue=5 |pages=521–549 |doi=10.1007/s00191-006-0054-0|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="march">{{cite journal |last1=Janzen |first1=Daniel H. |title=Costa Rica's Area de Conservación Guanacaste: A long march to survival through non-damaging biodevelopment |journal=Biodiversity |date=May 2000 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=7–20 |doi=10.1080/14888386.2000.9712501 |s2cid=129440404 |url=https://www.studocu.com/en/document/university-of-pennsylvania/humans-and-their-environments/other/a-long-march-to-survival-through-non-damaging-biodevelopment/727759/view |url-access=subscription |archive-date=October 24, 2019 |access-date=October 24, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191024153423/https://www.studocu.com/en/document/university-of-pennsylvania/humans-and-their-environments/other/a-long-march-to-survival-through-non-damaging-biodevelopment/727759/view }}</ref>

For this reason ACG was conceived as a cultural restoration project, which, to paraphrase its natural counterpart, ought to be grown as well. ACG integrates complementary processes of experimentation, [[Restoration ecology|habitat restoration]] and cultural development.<ref name="Allen"/>{{rp|89–91}}<ref name="Derroire">{{cite book |last1=Derroire |first1=Géraldine |title=Secondary succession in tropical dry forests drivers and mechanisms of forest regeneration Secondary succession in tropical dry forests. (Dissertation) |date=2016 |publisher=Sveriges lantbruksuniv Acta Universitatis Agriculturae Sueciae, 1652-6880 |location=Alnarp |isbn=978-91-576-8634-3 |url=https://pub.epsilon.slu.se/13400/1/derroire_g_160522.pdf}}</ref>
The techniques used include: 
* Active restoration, artificial dispersal of propagules from plant species native to the Guanacaste habitats<ref name="Derroire"/>{{rp|57,73}}
* Passive restoration by means of fire, anti-poaching and herbivore control<ref name="Derroire"/>{{rp|33,73}}
* Ecological education and sensibilisation<ref name="Allen"/>{{rp|275}}<ref name="Singer">{{cite book |last1=Singer |first1=F. D. |title=Ecology in Action|chapter=Chapter 18: Dan Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs: Community Interactions and Tropical Restoration through Biodiversity Conservation |date=2016 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-11537-8 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9mSSCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA467 |access-date=October 18, 2019}}</ref><ref name="Cruz">{{cite journal |last1=Cruz |first1=R. E. |last2=Blanco Segura |first2=R. |title=Developing the Bioliteracy of School Children for 24 Years: A Fundamental Tool for Ecological Restoration and Conservation in Perpetuity of the Área de Conservación Guanacaste, Costa Rica |journal=Ecological Restoration |date=2010 |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=193–198 |url=https://www.muse.jhu.edu/article/382395 |access-date=October 18, 2019|doi=10.3368/er.28.2.193 |s2cid=219193472 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Kazmier">{{cite web |last1=Kazmier |first1=Robin |title=The Parataxonomist Revolution: How a Group of Rural Costa Ricans Discovered 10,000 New Species |website=Comparative Media Studies: Science Writing |date=June 15, 2017 |url=https://cmsw.mit.edu/parataxonomist-revolution-group-rural-costa-ricans-discovered-10000-new-species/}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Janzen is married to ecologist [[Winifred Hallwachs]], who is also his frequent research partner. Of Hallwachs, Janzen has said, "We did these things together,"<ref name="Allen"/>{{rp|132–136}} and "we are very much together in perceiving things the same things....Since I'm the vocal member, it's then attributed to me. But I would say these ideas and directions and thoughts and actions are easily fifty-fifty attributable."<ref name="Allen"/>{{rp|134}}

==Honorary distinctions==
Janzen has been subject to recognition many times in the US, as well as in Europe and Latin America; the monetary endowments of these prizes have been invested in the trust fund of the ACG or another of his conservation's projects in Costa Rica. Prizes and distinctions garnered by Janzen include:
* 1975, The Henry Allan Gleason Award, [[Botanical Society of America]]
* 1984, [[Crafoord Prize]]: Coevolutionary ecology. [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{cite web |title=The Crafoord Prize 1984 – in ecology |url=https://www.crafoordprize.se/press_release/the-crafoord-prize-1984-in-ecology |website=The Crafoord Prize |date=August 31, 1984 |access-date=October 24, 2019}}</ref>
* 1985, Distinguished Teaching Award, [[University of Pennsylvania]]<ref name="Fishman">{{cite news |last1=Fishman |first1=Margie |title=Bio Prof Janzen garners 'Japanese Nobel Prize' for conservation work |url=https://www.thedp.com/article/1997/09/bio_prof_janzen_garners_japanese_nobel_prize_for_conservation_work |access-date=October 24, 2019 |work=The Daily Pennsylvanian |date=September 22, 1997}}</ref>
* 1987, The Berkeley Citation for Distinguished Achievement and Notable Service to the University,<ref>{{cite web |title=Berkeley Citation – Past Recipients |url=https://awards.berkeley.edu/berkeley-citation/recipients |website=Berkeley Awards |access-date=October 24, 2019}}</ref>  [[University of California, Berkeley]]
* 1987, Hijo Ilustre de Guanacaste (awarded by the Governor of [[Guanacaste province]])<ref name="Ciencias"/>
* 1987, [[Global 500 Roll of Honour]], [[UNEP]]<ref name="Allen"/>
* 1989, [[MacArthur Fellowship]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Meet the 1989 MacArthur Fellows |url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/class/august-1989/ |website=MacArthur Foundation |access-date=October 24, 2019}}</ref>
* 1989, [[Leidy Award]], Philadelphia Academy of Natural Sciences<ref name="PANSP">{{cite journal|date=June 2007|title=The Four Awards Bestowed by The Academy of Natural Sciences and Their Recipients|journal=Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia|publisher=The Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia|volume=156|issue=1|pages=403–404|doi=10.1635/0097-3157(2007)156[403:TFABBT]2.0.CO;2|s2cid=198160356 }}<!--|access-date=15 April 2015--></ref>
* 1991, Founder's Council Award of Merit, [[Field Museum of Natural History]]<ref>{{cite news |title=Founders' Council Award to Daniel H. Janzen, Ecologist |url=https://archive.org/details/field62A/page/2 |access-date=October 24, 2019 |work=In the field : the bulletin of the Field Museum of Natural History |issue=2|volume= 62|page=2 |publisher=Field Museum of Natural History |date=1991}}</ref>
* 1992, Member, [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]], USA<ref>{{cite web |title=Daniel H. Janzen |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/daniel-h-janzen-fsmmzm/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=October 24, 2019}}</ref>
* 1993, Award for Improvement of Costa Rican Quality of Life, [[Universidad de Costa Rica]] (co award with W. Hallwachs).<ref name="Allen">{{cite book |last1=Allen |first1=William |title=Green Phoenix: Restoring the Tropical Forests of Guanacaste |date=2001 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-516177-9 |pages=132–136|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8Ho8DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA132 }}</ref>
